source.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
source.authors: Bo Gong; Shiyang Lai; James Evans; D. Song

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how many distinct SAE feature clusters are strongly connected to neurons in two language models, and separately tests whether low-semantic-similarity, high-interference feature pairs are judged related. These are different measurements from the original vision-neuron examples.
record.gate_note: The study also reports feature-, token-gradient-, prompt-, and neuron-level interventions that deliberately steer outputs, plus transfer to larger models. Those induced shifts do not establish how often models spontaneously show the behavior in the claim versions. The neuron-intervention results are recorded under fits_no_version. The study's count of neurons connected to one or two feature clusters is not assigned to a particular model, so it is not recorded as a model-specific row.
record.test_reason: Beyond its intervention experiments, which use polysemanticity as a tool, the study measures the share of neurons in Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small that connect strongly to several distinct SAE feature clusters (Appendix N, Fig. 17). That is a different method aimed at V2's prevalence question. Its feature-pair relatedness annotations concern SAE features that share activation directions, not neurons, so they do not measure V6 as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude three things. First, steering with semantically unrelated but interfering SAE features, token gradients or prompts shifts next-token predictions toward a target, and these interventions transfer to larger instruction-tuned models. Second, polysemantic interference is therefore structured and not purely stochastic. Third, fewer than 30% of shared interference pairs have human-legible higher-order relations, and neuron output sensitivity grows with polysemanticity, with asymmetric super-neuron effects.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE-derived feature clustering and neuron-to-feature connections, then measures relatedness judgments and intervention effects; it does not reproduce the original vision-neuron activation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The study varies semantic-similarity cutoffs in intervention analyses and uses two different feature-pair judges; the judges' relatedness rates differ. Neuron counts use a stated feature-clustering cutoff of 0.4 and connection threshold >0.2.

fits_no_version.finding: Among shared high-interference, low-similarity SAE feature pairs, only 27.7% were judged by at least one LLM annotator to have a plausible higher-order association. Per-judge rates were 3.7–28.7%, with Cohen's kappa 0.22–0.41. In paired choices, GPT-5-mini picked the high-interference pair as more related 64.3% of the time versus similarity-matched low-interference pairs (CI 0.628–0.658).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features that share activation directions in small LMs are modestly more latently related than similarity-matched non-interfering pairs, but most such pairs lack a human-legible relation.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling neurons grouped by number of connected feature clusters shifts output semantics more for higher-degree neurons. 'Super-neurons' (>500 connections) show weak masking effects but large amplification effects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small, neurons connected to more aggregated SAE feature clusters have greater influence on output semantics when amplified, with asymmetric effects for super-neurons.

record.problems: The neuron definition depends on SAE feature clustering and a connection threshold; the neuron-distribution percentages are given without exact per-layer values in the text. Relatedness judgments are model-generated and the annotators have limited agreement. The paper's intervention evidence mainly concerns next-token shifts, and its own limitations note that transferability and downstream effects need further testing.
record.rows_left_out: No separately assignable model-specific value was reported for the statement that neurons connected to one or two aggregated features account for more than 33% among strongly connected neurons; the text does not identify the model or models for that aggregate. The cross-model prompt and gradient interventions and HellaSwag results were left out because the behaviors were deliberately induced and do not measure the versions' stated spontaneous response or neuron-meaning claims.

untested.parts: No direct activation-based test of neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts. No restriction to MLP neurons is stated. No layer-by-layer contrast is reported in text. No models larger than GPT-2-Small.
Assumes superposition (cites Elhage et al.) but does not test feature count versus neuron capacity as the cause.
No manipulation of initialization, regularization, noise or capacity.
No comparison across activation functions, architectures or regularization of the share of polysemantic neurons.
No re-examination of canonical polysemantic neurons with better tools. The feature-pair annotation concerns SAE features, not neurons.

The neuron count uses a single clustering cutoff (0.4) and connection threshold (0.2). Sensitivity of the neuron classification to these choices, activation range or explanation scoring is not tested.

missing.what: Degree distribution of strongly connected neurons, including 'super-neurons' with over 500 connected features. Shows a minority of neurons that are extremely polysemantic under the SAE criterion.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 labels were removed. The annotation concerns SAE feature pairs pre-filtered for low gloss similarity, not neurons. That makes 'mostly unrelated' partly a product of selection, and the judges are LLMs with low kappa. The reader's V2 'challenges' label was downgraded to limits_scope. The <5% figure rests on a restrictive top-3-neurons-per-cluster criterion, may include non-MLP sub-modules, and the authors themselves call polysemanticity pervasive. The intervention, transfer and HellaSwag results deliberately induce output shifts and use polysemanticity as a tool, so they are not tests of any version.

versions.untested_parts: Vision classifiers and InceptionV1 neuron examples.

The study measures strong neuron-to-feature-cluster connections in Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small, not response rates to unrelated token or context sets across language-model layers. It does not establish prevalence in larger language models.
The study does not test whether feature count exceeds neuron capacity or whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
No comparison of initialization, regularization, training noise, or sufficient neuron capacity.
No controlled comparison of activation functions, architectures, or regularization for the share of polysemantic neurons or performance cost.
The relatedness assessment concerns selected SAE feature pairs, not canonical individual neurons or direct neuron explanations; judgments come from language models rather than human raters.

The study varies semantic-similarity cutoffs and reports alternative intervention metrics, but does not test activation-range choices or how explanation-scoring choices change the classification of neurons.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Count neurons with strong connections to multiple aggregated SAE feature clusters.
rows.measure: Share of neurons identified as polysemantic by strong connections to aggregated features
rows.uncertainty: Figure 17 reports 95% error bars; exact bounds not stated
rows.note: The text explicitly states the fewer-than-5% result; it defines polysemantic neurons using strong connections to aggregated SAE features.
rows.check: Under a restrictive criterion, polysemantic neurons are under 5% per layer: only the top 3 neurons per cluster, connection >0.2, clusters at cosine 0.4. This is a much smaller share than V2 describes. The criterion caps detection, so 'absent' overstates it. The layers may include residual and attention sub-modules, not only MLPs. The per-layer value is stated jointly for both models.

tranche.reason: Appendix N uses a different method (SAE feature-neuron connections) on V2's prevalence question. The main work is interventions.

source_check.notes: 'Polysemantic neurons' in Appendix N means the top 3 neurons per SAE cluster with connection >0.2. No multi-cluster requirement is stated, and the set includes neurons tied to only 1 or 2 clusters. 'Neurons' are activation dimensions of any sub-module, not only MLP neurons. Code is released (App. Q), so the record's code: n is wrong. The rows' op text says 'multiple clusters', which the text does not state.

statements.correction: Appendix N: the analysis covers the top 3 neurons by alignment per SAE feature cluster (clusters at cosine 0.4, Sec. 3.6) and drops connections of 0.2 or less. Those 'polysemantic neurons with strong connections' are fewer than 5% in each layer of Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small (Fig. 17, 95% CIs). No several-cluster requirement is stated. Sec. 3.6: neurons linked to only 1 or 2 aggregated features are over 33% of strongly connected neurons.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the text never requires a neuron to connect to several clusters. Appendix N counts the top 3 neurons per cluster with connection >0.2, and Sec. 3.6 counts neurons linked to only 1 or 2 aggregated features among the strongly connected ones.
